subject: chemistry

moments.title: Pauling predicts noble gas compounds
moments.body:
Pauling speculates that the heavier noble gases — krypton, xenon, radon — should be able to form compounds with fluorine. He suggests XeF6 and KrF6 should exist.

No one tries seriously. The experimental challenges are formidable: fluorine is dangerous, xenon is expensive, and the experimental consensus says noble gases don't react.
moments.takeaway: A theoretical prediction sits unexamined for nearly 30 years.

moments.title: Bartlett notices a match of ionisation energies
moments.who: Neil Bartlett, University of British Columbia
moments.body:
Bartlett is working with platinum hexafluoride (PtF6), an extraordinarily strong oxidiser. He notices a sample turns red on contact with air. Analysis: PtF6 has stripped an electron from O2, giving O2+ PtF6-.

He looks up the relevant ionisation energies: O2 is 1175 kJ/mol; xenon is 1170 kJ/mol. Almost the same. He reasons that PtF6 should also be able to oxidise xenon.
moments.takeaway: An almost-coincidental match of two numbers points to a new chemistry.

moments.title: The first noble gas compound
moments.who: Neil Bartlett, University of British Columbia
moments.body:
On 23 March 1962 (later widely reported as June 1962 when the paper appeared), Bartlett combines xenon gas with PtF6 vapour in a glass apparatus. The reaction is instantaneous — a yellow solid forms.

He characterises it as Xe+[PtF6]- (later shown to be more complex). The first compound of a noble gas exists.

quote.text: I had to look twice to believe it.
quote.attrib: Neil Bartlett, on the first XePtF6 product

moments.takeaway: The 'inert gases' are not entirely inert. A six-decade-old chemistry orthodoxy falls.

moments.title: An entire new chemistry opens
moments.who: Argonne, Oak Ridge, Berkeley and others
moments.body:
Within months, Claassen, Selig and Malm at Argonne produce XeF4 by simply heating xenon with fluorine at 400°C in a nickel container. XeF2 (Hoppe, Münster) and XeF6 (Slivnik, Ljubljana) follow within two years.

XeO3 (an explosive oxide), KrF2 and ClO3+ F- soon follow. The full set of compounds maps the noble gases' chemistry from element 36 (krypton) onwards.
moments.takeaway: A whole chemistry — written off as impossible — opens up in two years.

now.title: Noble gas chemistry today
now.body:
Xenon and krypton have rich chemistry: oxides, fluorides, oxyfluorides and even Xe-N, Xe-C bonded compounds. Radon is too radioactive to study extensively but is known to form RnF2. Argon forms HArF only at cryogenic temperatures (Helsinki, 2000).

Xenon difluoride is used as a selective oxidising/fluorinating agent in organic synthesis. Excimer lasers (KrF, ArF, XeCl) use noble gas chemistry to produce intense UV light.
now.open_questions: Can helium and neon ever form stable compounds in normal conditions? Recent calculations suggest Na2He may be stable at very high pressures (predicted 2014, possibly observed 2017). Can predictive computational chemistry guide synthesis of new noble gas compounds?

reflection: From 1933 to 1962, the prediction that xenon should form compounds was on the books. No one tried seriously for nearly 30 years because everyone knew noble gases were inert. How often does scientific orthodoxy keep researchers from attempting experiments that turn out to be both feasible and revolutionary?
